notes:
I've got notes for most verses. My research tools ran out before I could read a page for every verse, so some verses rest on only one or two sources. I found nothing on bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, the Orthodox site (oca.org) or the Pentecostal and Lutheran sites other than Enduring Word. I also found no page that directly discusses prosperity or word-of-faith readings of this chapter. Where a source names a commentator's tradition, I've included it.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says that in ancient Israel the barren woman carried an enormous load of shame and disgrace, and the Lord compares captive Israel to her. He adds that Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 4:27 about the "birth" of New Covenant believers, and probably meant that they would outnumber the children of the Old Covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/
- The Pulpit Commentary says exiled Israel is called "barren" because in the time of suffering, her numbers rather diminished than increased. Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran) see Jerusalem as matching Sarah, barren at first and fruitful later. Barnes (Presbyterian) thinks the saying may be proverbial for a much greater increase than expected, fulfilled when the Gentiles join (v. 3). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-1.html
- **Where traditions differ (Israel or the church?):**
  - *Reformed:* Calvin calls the Church "barren" because it could expect no children so long as she groaned under wretched bondage. He notes she is called both barren and a widow, a double hopelessness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-1.html On Galatians, Calvin says Isaiah speaks of the kingdom of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom41/calcom41.iii.vi.v.html
  - *Baptist:* Gill follows Paul and applies the verse to the gospel church, which was like a barren woman before Pentecost because it had so few converts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-1.html
  - *Methodist:* Benson says the verse speaks to the church as God's spouse, made up first of Jews and then of Gentiles. He says she was "barren" before Christ came because there were few sincere converts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/54-1.htm
  - *Dispensational:* J. Vernon McGee says that here it is the nation Israel, a restored wife, as opposed to the church, which he calls a chaste virgin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-1.html Constable reads Paul's use of the verse as probably pointing to the blessings of the millennial kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/4-27.html
- **Other views:**
  - *Catholic:* Haydock takes "barren" as the Jews in captivity, or the Church of the Gentiles, to which alone the expressions can be applied. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-1.html
  - *Older critical scholarship:* Meyer says the historical sense is the joyful promise of a great increase to the depressed people of God after the exile. Ellicott says Paul applies words first spoken of Jerusalem to the persecuted early Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/galatians/4-27.htm

**vv. 2–3**
- Guzik says Israel would be so fruitful it would need more living space. This would encourage returning exiles who felt few and weak. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/
- A Bible Hub article reads the enlarged tent as a picture of safety under God's covering. It takes "spread out to the right and left" as geographic and ethnic expansion, and links "dispossess" to the land promised to Abraham. It also applies v. 2 to church planting. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_the_barren_woman_important.htm
- Barnes sees v. 3 as fulfilled when the Gentiles join. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-1.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik compares Israel's humiliation to the shame of widowhood, which the Lord promises to remove. He quotes Motyer that the three words for shame share the idea of disappointed hopes, meaning you expect one thing publicly and get another. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/
- The Biblical Illustrator says that for the Hebrew church, the bondage in Egypt was "the shame of her youth" and the captivity in Babylon was "the reproach of her widowhood." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-1.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik says God is not just a husband but a great one, and lists the titles in the verse as proof. He applies the verse personally to women who have been abandoned, saying God can meet emotional needs when others forsake us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/
- Gill notes that Jewish writers themselves apply "thy Maker is thy husband" to the time of the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/6-45.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik takes vv. 4–6 together: God restores Israel like a rescued widow, removing her disgrace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik says God never really forsook Israel, but He recognised that they *felt* forsaken. The forsaking is brief, while the kindness is everlasting. When we feel abandoned, we should see it as only "a moment." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/

**v. 9**
- Guzik: just as Noah's flood waters went down, God's anger toward Israel will go down. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/
- Benson and Poole say this covenant will be as certain and lasting as the one with Noah. God promises not to be angry "so as to forsake thee utterly." Ellicott notes this is one of the few Old Testament references to the Flood outside Genesis, and that Genesis 9 calls it a "covenant" rather than an "oath," though for God the two are nearly the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/54-9.htm
- GotQuestions says the judgment is "like the waters of Noah" because it is temporary and will end in deliverance. https://www.gotquestions.org/waters-of-Noah.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik: God's kindness is more certain than the mountains. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/
- Calvin says it is called a "covenant of peace" because it offers all that belongs to perfect happiness. Constable thinks it probably refers to the New Covenant, and quotes Motyer's link between the Servant's work and the covenant with Noah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-10.html
- Gill applies it to the new covenant, made in Christ's blood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/54-10.htm
- **A point that divides readers:** One commentary on that page says God will not reject the Christian Church as he cast off the Church of the Jews. Readers who see the promise as still pointing to Israel would not read it that way (see the dispensational views under v. 1 and v. 17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/54-9.htm

**vv. 11–12**
- Guzik: God cares for the afflicted who feel uncomforted. The jewels mean He will make the afflicted truly rich, even if they feel poor whatever their bank balance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/
- Matthew Henry reads the precious stones as the beauty of the "gospel temple," produced by the power of its doctrines. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-12.html
- Keil & Delitzsch say the city's outward glory only shows the spiritual glory of the church living in it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-13.html

**v. 13**
- **Traditional reading:** Jesus quotes this verse in John 6:45. Ellicott (Anglican) says it means more precisely "disciples of Jehovah," fulfilled in Christ's disciples. Constable says Jesus saw a preview of this in His own ministry. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-13.html Barnes links it to Jeremiah 31:34. Poole says "peace" includes inward and outward peace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/54-13.htm Henry says God takes the teaching of the church's many children into His own hands. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_054.cfm
- **Where traditions differ (how does God's teaching work?):**
  - *Reformed (Calvin):* The teaching cannot mean outward preaching alone, because preaching does not make everyone believe. Only those who "have been foreordained to life" are truly teachable. Calvin explicitly opposes views that make grace depend on free will. He also says Isaiah joins inward and outward teaching, since the church's children are nourished by her. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-13.html On John 6:45 he says "all" must be limited to the elect. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/6-45.html
  - *Methodist:* Wesley and Benson say God teaches outwardly by His word and inwardly by His Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-13.html Clarke says on John 6:45 that God draws people by His love: fear pushes away, love attracts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/6-45.html
  - *Presbyterian (Barnes, differing from Calvin):* On John 6:45 Barnes says this drawing is not compulsory; the only barrier is people's own unwillingness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/6-45.html
  - *Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):* Jerusalem's children will need no human instruction but carry heaven's teaching within them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-13.html
- **Popular application:** Bible Hub's study notes say true prosperity is not merely material; the word behind it is shalom. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/54-13.htm

**v. 14**
- Guzik: the afflicted will find protection and security in God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/
- The Biblical Illustrator calls righteousness the city's foundation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-12.html

**v. 15**
- Guzik takes vv. 14–15 together: enemies may gather, but not by God's will, and they will fall. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/
- Bible Hub cites v. 15 to show that v. 17 does not promise believers will never face opposition. https://biblehub.com/q/What_does_Isaiah_54_17_mean.htm

**v. 16**
- GotQuestions: God made the one who makes the weapons, so God is in charge. https://www.gotquestions.org/no-weapon-formed-against-you-shall-prosper.html
- Keil & Delitzsch say the same creative power that lies behind the weapon has already provided a defender of Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/54-17.htm

**v. 17**
- **Traditional reading:** Barnes says "prosper" means the weapon will have no *final* success; persecutors may seem to succeed for a while. He thinks the "tongue" language comes from the law courts. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/dby/isaiah/54-17.html
- Gill applies the verse to the failure of Rome's persecutions, recalling the saying that the martyrs' blood was the seed of the church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/54-17.htm
- Spurgeon (Baptist) applies it to every true believer personally, and says each wave of persecution left the church more glorious. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-17.html
- **Limits on the promise:** Guzik says it is not a blanket promise for any churchgoer; it belongs to the Lord's servants whose righteousness comes from Him. Sometimes God lets the weapon strike and brings greater good out of it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-54/ Bible Hub calls these promises not blank checks for the rebellious. https://biblehub.com/q/What_does_Isaiah_54_17_mean.htm
- **Who is it for?** GotQuestions says it will be ultimately fulfilled in Christ's millennial kingdom but is often applied to God's children today facing spiritual enemies. https://www.gotquestions.org/no-weapon-formed-against-you-shall-prosper.html Constable places it in a future peaceful era. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/54-17.html
- **"Their righteousness/vindication is from Me":** Bible Hub links this to justification (Romans 8:33–34). https://biblehub.com/study/isaiah/54-17.htm
